title: NOx Trap Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 1
plain: The NOx trap (a special catalytic converter that stores and burns off nitrogen oxide pollution) on bank 1 (the side of the engine with cylinder 1) isn't working as well as it should. This is found on some diesel and lean-burn gasoline engines.
symptoms: Usually no change in how the car drives

causes.name: Worn-out or sulfur-contaminated NOx trap
Faulty NOx sensor
Exhaust leak near the sensors
Engine running rich or burning oil

checks: Check for exhaust leaks and other engine codes first
Check NOx sensor readings in live data
Use high-quality, low-sulfur fuel and let the system run a cleaning cycle
fix: Fix sensor or leak problems first; a worn NOx trap has to be replaced.

title: NOx Trap Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 2
plain: The NOx trap (a special catalytic converter that stores and burns off nitrogen oxide pollution) on bank 2 (the side of the engine opposite cylinder 1) isn't working as well as it should. This is found on some diesel and lean-burn gasoline engines.
symptoms: Usually no change in how the car drives

causes.name: Worn-out or sulfur-contaminated NOx trap
Faulty NOx sensor
Exhaust leak near the sensors
Engine running rich or burning oil

checks: Check for exhaust leaks and other engine codes first
Check NOx sensor readings in live data
Use high-quality, low-sulfur fuel and let the system run a cleaning cycle
fix: Fix sensor or leak problems first; a worn NOx trap has to be replaced.

title: Diesel Particulate Filter Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 1
plain: The computer thinks the diesel particulate filter (DPF) on bank 1 isn't trapping soot like it should. Most often the filter is cracked or the pressure sensor that watches it is giving bad readings.
symptoms: Possible black smoke or soot at the tailpipe

causes.name: Cracked or damaged diesel particulate filter
Faulty DPF differential pressure sensor
Cracked, loose or plugged DPF pressure sensor hoses
Exhaust leak before the filter
Filter removed or tampered with

checks: Inspect the DPF pressure sensor hoses for cracks or soot buildup
Compare DPF pressure readings in live data at idle and higher RPM
Look for soot at the tailpipe, which points to a cracked filter
fix: Repair hoses or the pressure sensor if they are bad; a cracked filter must be replaced.
drive: Usually drivable short term, but don't ignore it. If you see heavy black smoke, power drops a lot, or a message says the filter is full, get it checked soon. If you smell burning or see smoke from underneath, pull over and shut it off, as exhaust parts can get very hot.
test_first: Check the filter pressure sensor and its hoses, look for exhaust leaks and soot after the filter, and review regeneration history before replacing the particulate filter.

title: Diesel Particulate Filter Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 2
plain: The computer thinks the diesel particulate filter (DPF) on bank 2 isn't trapping soot like it should, usually from a cracked filter or bad pressure readings.
symptoms: Possible black smoke at the tailpipe

causes.name: Cracked or damaged diesel particulate filter
Faulty DPF pressure sensor or hoses
Exhaust leak before the filter

checks: Inspect DPF pressure sensor hoses
Compare DPF pressure readings in live data
fix: Repair the pressure sensor or hoses if faulty; replace the filter if it is cracked.

title: Intake Manifold Runner Control Stuck Open Bank 1
plain: The flaps inside the intake manifold on bank 1 (the side of the engine with cylinder 1) seem stuck open. These flaps change how air flows into the engine to help power at different speeds.
symptoms: Weaker power at low engine speeds
Rough or uneven idle in some cases
Possible rattle or ticking from the intake

causes.name: Intake runner flaps or linkage stuck with carbon buildup
Failed intake manifold runner actuator
Broken flap, shaft or linkage inside the manifold
Vacuum leak to a vacuum-operated actuator
Wiring or connector fault at the actuator

checks: Watch the actuator move (or not) when the engine is started or revved
Check vacuum lines to the actuator if it is vacuum-operated
Look for broken linkage or a binding flap shaft
fix: Clean or free up the runner flaps if possible; often the actuator or the whole intake manifold has to be replaced.
examples: Well known on Mercedes-Benz V6 and V8 engines (M272/M273) with intake manifold flap problems
drive: It usually doesn't change how the car drives while you arrange a repair; low-speed power may be weaker or idle rough. If you hear loud rattling from the intake or the engine starts misfiring or running poorly, get it checked sooner, since broken runner parts can be pulled into the engine on some designs.
test_first: Command the runner control on and off with a scanner and watch it move; check the vacuum supply or motor, linkage and position sensor, and look for broken runner parts.

title: Intake Manifold Runner Control Stuck Open Bank 2
plain: The flaps inside the intake manifold on bank 2 (the side of the engine opposite cylinder 1) seem stuck open. These flaps change how air flows into the engine to help power at different speeds.
symptoms: Weaker power at low engine speeds
Rough or uneven idle in some cases

causes.name: Intake runner flaps or linkage stuck with carbon buildup
Failed intake manifold runner actuator
Broken flap, shaft or linkage inside the manifold
Vacuum leak to a vacuum-operated actuator

checks: Watch the actuator move (or not) when the engine is started or revved
Check vacuum lines to the actuator if it is vacuum-operated
fix: Clean or free up the runner flaps if possible; often the actuator or the whole intake manifold has to be replaced.

plain: The flaps inside the intake manifold on bank 1 (the side of the engine with cylinder 1) seem stuck closed. These flaps change how air flows into the engine to help power at different speeds.
symptoms: Weaker power at higher engine speeds
Rough or uneven idle in some cases
Possible rattle or ticking from the intake

causes.name: Intake runner flaps or linkage stuck with carbon buildup
Failed intake manifold runner actuator
Broken flap, shaft or linkage inside the manifold
Vacuum leak to a vacuum-operated actuator
Wiring or connector fault at the actuator

checks: Watch the actuator move (or not) when the engine is started or revved
Check vacuum lines to the actuator if it is vacuum-operated
Look for broken linkage or a binding flap shaft
fix: Clean or free up the runner flaps if possible; often the actuator or the whole intake manifold has to be replaced.
drive: Usually drivable while you arrange a repair, with weaker power at higher RPM. If the engine misfires, runs rough or you hear loud rattling from the intake, get it checked sooner, since broken parts could be drawn into the engine on some designs.
test_first: Check whether the runners move when commanded and inspect for carbon buildup, a seized shaft, a failed actuator or a vacuum leak, and verify the position sensor before replacing the manifold.

title: Intake Manifold Runner Control Stuck Closed Bank 2
plain: The flaps inside the intake manifold on bank 2 (the side of the engine opposite cylinder 1) seem stuck closed. These flaps change how air flows into the engine to help power at different speeds.
symptoms: Weaker power at higher engine speeds
Rough or uneven idle in some cases

title: Intake Manifold Runner Control Circuit/Open Bank 1
plain: The engine computer can't properly control the intake manifold runner control on bank 1, which moves flaps in the intake to change how air flows into the engine. It sees an open or broken circuit, often from wiring, a connector or the part itself.
symptoms: Slightly weaker power at some engine speeds

causes.name: Failed intake manifold runner control actuator
Broken wire or unplugged connector
Blown fuse or bad relay feeding the circuit
Engine computer driver problem (rare)

checks: Inspect the runner control actuator connector and wiring
Check for power at the connector and measure the part's resistance
fix: Repair any wiring fault first; if the wiring tests good, replace the intake manifold runner control actuator.

title: Intake Manifold Runner Control Circuit Low Bank 1
plain: The control circuit for the intake manifold runner control on bank 1 is reading low voltage. This part moves flaps in the intake to change how air flows into the engine. A wire shorted to ground or a shorted part is the usual reason.
symptoms: Slightly weaker power at some engine speeds

causes.name: Control wire shorted to ground
Internally shorted intake manifold runner control actuator
Damaged connector
Engine computer driver problem (rare)

checks: Check the runner control actuator wiring for rubbed-through insulation
Measure the runner control actuator resistance and compare with spec
fix: Repair any wiring fault first; if the wiring tests good, replace the intake manifold runner control actuator.

title: Intake Manifold Runner Performance Bank 1
plain: The intake runner flaps on bank 1 (the side of the engine with cylinder 1) aren't moving the way the computer commands. They may be sticking, slow or not reaching the right position.
symptoms: Slightly weaker power at some engine speeds

causes.name: Carbon buildup making the flaps stick
Worn or failed runner actuator
Broken linkage or flap shaft
Vacuum leak on a vacuum-operated system

checks: Watch the actuator and linkage move with a scan tool command
Check for vacuum leaks or broken linkage
fix: Free up or repair the flaps and linkage; replace the actuator or intake manifold if worn.

title: Intake Manifold Runner Performance Bank 2
plain: The intake runner flaps on bank 2 (the side of the engine opposite cylinder 1) aren't moving the way the computer commands. They may be sticking, slow or not reaching the right position.
symptoms: Slightly weaker power at some engine speeds

causes.name: Carbon buildup making the flaps stick
Worn or failed runner actuator
Broken linkage or flap shaft
Vacuum leak on a vacuum-operated system

checks: Watch the actuator and linkage move with a scan tool command
Check for vacuum leaks or broken linkage
fix: Free up or repair the flaps and linkage; replace the actuator or intake manifold if worn.

title: Diesel Particulate Filter Over Temperature Bank 1
plain: The diesel particulate filter on bank 1 (the side of the engine with cylinder 1) got hotter than it should. This can happen during a soot burn-off when too much soot or extra fuel burns at once.

causes.name: Too much soot in the filter burning at once
Leaking or dripping fuel injector adding raw fuel
Faulty exhaust temperature sensor
Oil getting into the exhaust from a turbo or engine problem

checks: Check exhaust temperature sensor readings
Check for leaking injectors or oil getting into the exhaust
fix: Fix the source of extra fuel or soot, then check the filter for heat damage; replace the filter if it is cracked.

title: Diesel Particulate Filter Over Temperature Bank 2
plain: The diesel particulate filter on bank 2 (the side of the engine opposite cylinder 1) got hotter than it should. This can happen during a soot burn-off when too much soot or extra fuel burns at once.

checks: Check exhaust temperature sensor readings

fix: Fix the source of extra fuel or soot, then check the filter for heat damage; replace the filter if it is cracked.

title: Catalyst System Over Temperature Bank 1
plain: The catalytic converter on bank 1 (the side of the engine with cylinder 1) is running too hot. Unburned fuel from a misfire or rich running is usually burning inside it.
symptoms: Possible rotten egg or burning smell

causes.name: Engine misfire sending unburned fuel into the exhaust
Engine running too rich
Faulty exhaust temperature sensor
Leaking fuel injector

checks: Check for misfire and fuel trim codes and fix them first
Check exhaust temperature sensor readings
fix: Fix the misfire or rich condition quickly; a converter that overheated may need replacing.

title: Catalyst System Over Temperature Bank 2
plain: The catalytic converter on bank 2 (the side of the engine opposite cylinder 1) is running too hot. Unburned fuel from a misfire or rich running is usually burning inside it.

Engine running too rich
Faulty exhaust temperature sensor
Leaking fuel injector

checks: Check for misfire and fuel trim codes and fix them first
Check exhaust temperature sensor readings
fix: Fix the misfire or rich condition quickly; a converter that overheated may need replacing.

title: Intake Manifold Runner Control Circuit High Bank 1
plain: The control circuit for the intake manifold runner control on bank 1 is reading high voltage. This part moves flaps in the intake to change how air flows into the engine. A wire shorted to power, an open circuit or a failed part is the usual reason.
symptoms: Slightly weaker power at some engine speeds

causes.name: Failed intake manifold runner control actuator
Control wire shorted to a power source
Open circuit or corroded connector
Engine computer driver problem (rare)

checks: Check the runner control actuator wiring for shorts to other wires
Measure the runner control actuator resistance and compare with spec
fix: Repair any wiring fault first; if the wiring tests good, replace the intake manifold runner control actuator.

title: Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Bank 1
plain: The engine computer has found a problem in the circuit for the intake manifold runner position sensor on bank 1, which tells the computer where the intake flaps are. It usually points to wiring, a connector or the sensor itself.
symptoms: Slightly weaker power at some engine speeds

causes.name: Faulty runner position sensor (often part of the actuator)
Damaged, corroded or unplugged connector
Broken or chafed wiring
Engine computer problem (rare)

checks: Inspect the runner position sensor connector and wiring for damage or corrosion
Check the sensor power, ground and signal with a meter
fix: Repair any damaged wiring or connector first; if the circuit tests good, replace the runner position sensor (often part of the actuator).

cost.job: Replace intake runner position sensor or actuator

title: Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1
plain: The sensor that reports the position of the intake manifold flaps on bank 1 is giving readings that don't match what the computer commanded. Often the flaps or their linkage are actually stuck or broken.
symptoms: Slightly weaker power at low or high speeds

causes.name: Broken or worn intake runner linkage or flap
Failed runner position sensor or actuator
Carbon buildup making the flaps stick
Wiring or connector problem
Vacuum leak on a vacuum-operated system

checks: Look at the runner linkage for a popped-off or broken arm
Watch the position reading change while commanding the flaps
Inspect the sensor connector and wiring
fix: Repair the linkage if possible; otherwise replace the actuator/sensor or, on some engines, the intake manifold.

cost.job: Replace intake runner actuator or intake manifold

examples: Very common on Mercedes-Benz M272 V6 engines and some VW/Audi 2.0T engines
drive: Usually drivable normally; most people notice little more than a slight change in power. Get it checked when convenient. If the engine starts running rough, misfiring or you hear rattling from the intake, have it looked at sooner.
test_first: Compare the runner position sensor reading to actual runner movement, and check the sensor wiring and linkage for wear or a broken clip before replacing the intake manifold.

title: Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Low Bank 1
plain: The signal from the intake manifold runner position sensor on bank 1 is lower than the computer expects. This sensor tells the computer where the intake flaps are. A wire shorted to ground or a failed sensor is the usual reason.
symptoms: Slightly weaker power at some engine speeds

causes.name: Signal or reference wire shorted to ground
Failed runner position sensor (often part of the actuator)
Corroded or damaged connector
Engine computer problem (rare)

checks: Inspect the runner position sensor wiring for rubbed-through or pinched spots
Unplug the sensor and see if the reading changes, which helps separate wiring from sensor
fix: Repair any damaged wiring or connector first; if the circuit tests good, replace the runner position sensor (often part of the actuator).

cost.job: Replace intake runner position sensor or actuator

title: Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor/Switch Circuit High Bank 1
plain: The signal from the intake manifold runner position sensor on bank 1 is higher than the computer expects. This sensor tells the computer where the intake flaps are. An open (broken) wire, a bad ground or a failed sensor is the usual reason.
symptoms: Slightly weaker power at some engine speeds

causes.name: Open or broken signal or ground wire
Unplugged or corroded connector
Failed runner position sensor (often part of the actuator)
Wire shorted to a power source

checks: Make sure the runner position sensor connector is fully plugged in and clean
Check the sensor ground and signal wire for an open circuit
fix: Repair any damaged wiring or connector first; if the circuit tests good, replace the runner position sensor (often part of the actuator).

cost.job: Replace intake runner position sensor or actuator

title: Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Intermittent Bank 1
plain: The signal from the intake manifold runner position sensor on bank 1 keeps dropping out or jumping around. This sensor tells the computer where the intake flaps are. A loose connection or a damaged wire is the usual reason.
symptoms: Slightly weaker power at some engine speeds

causes.name: Loose or corroded connector
Chafed wire that opens or shorts as the engine moves
Failing runner position sensor (often part of the actuator)

checks: Wiggle the harness and connector while watching live data for dropouts
Inspect the runner position sensor wiring along its whole route
fix: Repair any damaged wiring or connector first; if the circuit tests good, replace the runner position sensor (often part of the actuator).

cost.job: Replace intake runner position sensor or actuator

Check wiring and connector for corrosion or looseness
fix: Confirm the system itself is working, then replace the runner position sensor (often part of the actuator) if its readings are off.

title: Fuel Fired Heater Disabled
plain: The small fuel-burning heater that some diesel vehicles use to warm the cabin or engine has been shut off by the control system because of a fault.
symptoms: Slow cabin or engine warm-up in cold weather

causes.name: Auxiliary heater fault (glow pin, fuel pump or fan)
Low fuel level, which stops the heater from running
Wiring or fuse problem
Heater control module fault

checks: Check for other heater codes stored in the heater module
Check the heater fuse, fuel supply and exhaust outlet for blockage
fix: Repair the fault that disabled the heater; parts like the glow pin or dosing pump may need replacing.

title: Reductant Tank Heater Control Circuit/Open
plain: The engine computer can't properly control the reductant (DEF) tank heater, which warms the diesel exhaust fluid so it does not freeze. It sees an open or broken circuit, often from wiring, a connector or the part itself.
symptoms: DEF or emissions warning on the dash
A countdown to reduced speed may start if not repaired

causes.name: Failed DEF tank heater (often part of the tank sender)
Broken wire or unplugged connector
Blown fuse or bad relay feeding the circuit
Engine computer driver problem (rare)

checks: Inspect the DEF heater connector and wiring
Check for power at the connector and measure the part's resistance
fix: Repair any wiring fault first; if the wiring tests good, replace the DEF tank heater (often part of the tank sender).

cost.job: Replace DEF tank heater or sender

title: Reductant Tank Heater Control Circuit Low
plain: The control circuit for the reductant (DEF) tank heater is reading low voltage. This part warms the diesel exhaust fluid so it does not freeze. A wire shorted to ground or a shorted part is the usual reason.
symptoms: DEF or emissions warning on the dash
A countdown to reduced speed may start if not repaired

causes.name: Control wire shorted to ground
Internally shorted DEF tank heater (often part of the tank sender)
Damaged connector
Engine computer driver problem (rare)

checks: Check the DEF heater wiring for rubbed-through insulation
Measure the DEF heater resistance and compare with spec
fix: Repair any wiring fault first; if the wiring tests good, replace the DEF tank heater (often part of the tank sender).

cost.job: Replace DEF tank heater or sender

title: Reductant Leakage
plain: The system that sprays diesel exhaust fluid (DEF) into the exhaust has detected a leak somewhere in its lines or parts.
symptoms: DEF or emissions warning on the dash
A countdown to reduced speed may start if not repaired
White crystal buildup around DEF lines or injector

causes.name: Leaking DEF line or fitting
Leaking DEF injector seal
Cracked DEF tank or pump module

checks: Look for white crusty DEF deposits along the lines, pump and injector
Check that line fittings are tight and not cracked
fix: Repair the leaking line, fitting or component and clear the code.

title: Fuel Fired Heater Performance
plain: The fuel-burning auxiliary heater on this vehicle isn't producing heat the way it should.
symptoms: Little or no extra heat in cold weather

causes.name: Carbon-fouled burner or glow pin
Weak or failing heater fuel pump
Blocked heater exhaust or air intake
Heater control module fault

checks: Check the heater exhaust and intake for blockage
Read codes from the heater module itself
fix: Clean or service the auxiliary heater, replacing the glow pin, fuel pump or burner as needed.
